kernelIdea: x² ≥ 0 for every real x, so x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution. Roots of polynomials matter enough that mathematicians extended the number system rather than accept the gap.

kernels.l1: Counting numbers tell you how many. They do not turn you around — so people made a new number whose whole job is turning.
kernels.l2: Every square you can build holds a real, countable amount — never less than nothing. So no number, multiplied by itself, points you backwards, and that gap is what a new number was built to fill.
kernels.l3: No number on the number line, multiplied by itself, gives a negative answer. So x × x = −1 has no answer among the numbers we have, and mathematicians built a new number to answer it.
kernels.l4: For every x ∈ ℝ, x² ≥ 0, so x² = −1 has no real solution and x² + 1 has no real root. Rather than accept that gap, mathematicians extended ℝ — exactly as ℕ was extended to subtract and ℤ to divide.
kernels.l5: x² ≥ 0 on ℝ by case analysis, so x² + 1 is a real polynomial with no real root; the discriminant of the quadratic formula is where this gap is met in practice.
kernels.l6: The failure of ℝ to be algebraically closed is visible in the simplest possible case, x² + 1; extending the number system is the standard response to such a failure.
kernels.l7: Since x² ≥ 0 for all real x, the polynomial x² + 1 has no real root: ℝ is not algebraically closed. Extending the number system rather than accepting the gap is the same move that produced ℤ, ℚ, and ℝ.
kernels.l8: ℝ is not algebraically closed; ℂ is its algebraic closure, and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra says one extension suffices for every polynomial at once.
